drapeaux.note: Conan Doyle's text is English; the exchange is quoted word for word and was checked in the full text of The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes on Project Gutenberg (via a mirror, as gutenberg.org was down for maintenance).

All quoted lines from The Adventure of the Crooked Man (“I have the advantage of knowing your habits, my dear Watson,” “Excellent!”, “Elementary,” “my dear fellow,” “entirely meretricious”) and from Wodehouse's Psmith, Journalist are given in the original English, checked in the Project Gutenberg texts of both books; Gillette's “Oh, this is elementary, my dear fellow” is quoted as it appears on the English Wikipedia page “Sherlock Holmes” (allegedly from his 1899 play, present only in some versions), and was not checked in a script.

titre: “Elementary, My Dear Watson”: Conan Doyle Never Wrote It
accroche: Sherlock Holmes's most famous line appears in none of Conan Doyle's sixty adventures.
contenu_vulgarise:
Everyone knows it, and everyone attributes it to Sherlock Holmes: “Elementary, my dear Watson.” Yet if you open Conan Doyle's sixty stories, you will not find it there.

## What Is Really Written

The closest version is found in *The Adventure of the Crooked Man*, published in 1893 and then collected in *The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes*. Holmes deduces that Watson, whose boots are worn but clean, took a cab (a *hansom*) to make his rounds for the day. Watson exclaims: “Excellent!” Holmes replies: “Elementary.” The word is there. The “my dear Watson” is there too, but in the preceding line (“I have the advantage of knowing your habits, my dear Watson”). And in the line that contains “Elementary,” Holmes addresses his friend with a different term: “my dear fellow.”

The two pieces thus exist in the canon, separately. Never put together in a single line. The expression “my dear Watson” in fact recurs seventeen times in the *Memoirs* collection alone: the word “elementary” was simply never stuck to it.

## An “Elementary” Less Amiable Than the Legend

In the scene, the word is nothing like a polite formula. Holmes explains that such an effect seems remarkable to his neighbor only because the latter has missed the one little point that is the basis of the deduction. Then he turns the remark against his companion: the effect of Watson's little chronicles is, he says, “entirely meretricious,” because Watson keeps in his own hands some factors in the problem that he never imparts to the reader. The “elementary” of the text is thus a jab, which opens a literary reproach.

## Where the Phrase Comes From

It comes from elsewhere. According to Wikipedia, the phrase and its variants are found in newspaper articles as early as 1909, and P. G. Wodehouse uses it in *Psmith, Journalist*, serialized from 1909 to 1910: in the January 1910 installment, a character says “Elementary, my dear Watson, elementary.” It then settles into the ear of the general public with the films of the Rathbone-Bruce series, from 1939 to 1946. The play by William Gillette (1899) is also cited, in which Holmes would say “Oh, this is elementary, my dear fellow”; but the text of that play was reworked over three decades, and the phrase appears in some versions only.

## What This Shifts

A quotation does not need to be authentic to be true in everyone's eyes: it is enough that it sums up what people believe about a character. Doyle's Holmes is, moreover, drier than the one of legend: his “elementary” is a jab, which follows a compliment and precedes a reproach about Watson's accounts, which he judges “entirely meretricious.”

carte.punch: “Elementary, my dear Watson”: Conan Doyle never wrote that line.
carte.idee: In Conan Doyle's sixty stories, Holmes says “Elementary” and “my dear Watson,” but never in one breath. The complete phrase appears in the press as early as 1909, in Wodehouse in 1910, and then it takes hold with the movies.

quiz.question: Where do we find, as early as 1910, “Elementary, my dear Watson” in so many words?
choix: In The Adventure of the Crooked Man, from Conan Doyle's pen, in 1893
In a Wodehouse novel published in 1909-1910, not in Doyle's stories
In Doyle's first story, A Study in Scarlet, in 1887
In every version of William Gillette's play, in 1899
quiz.explication: Doyle's canon contains “Elementary” and “my dear Watson” separately. The complete phrase appears in the January 1910 installment of Wodehouse's novel, before being popularized by the movies; in Gillette, it appears only in some versions, in a different form.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When Holmes says “Elementary” in “The Crooked Man,” what comes before?
choix: Watson exclaims “Excellent!” after a deduction about his boots
Watson asks him to repeat his last sentence
Holmes has just solved the murder of Colonel Barclay
Lestrade admits he understands nothing about the case
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Holmes has just guessed, from Watson's boots, that he took a cab; Watson says “Excellent!” and Holmes replies “Elementary.”

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the line where Holmes says “Elementary,” how does he address Watson?
choix: He does not address him directly in that line
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that, in the line containing the word Elementary, Holmes calls his friend my dear fellow, not my dear Watson, which appears in the preceding line.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Holmes call Watson's chronicles “entirely meretricious”?
choix: Because Watson invents details that do not exist in the cases he recounts
Because Watson writes in a style Holmes finds too poetic
Because Watson keeps to himself factors in the problem that he never reveals to the reader
Because Watson publishes his stories without ever asking Holmes's permission
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Holmes turns the remark against Watson: his chronicles seem meretricious because he keeps to himself factors in the problem without ever handing them over to the reader.
